title: Han Xin's Army With Its Back to the River
text:
In 204 BC, during the war that founded the Han dynasty, the general Han Xin marched against the kingdom of Zhao through the Jingxing pass. Zhao's commander Chen Yu waited with a far larger army and ignored an adviser who urged him to cut Han Xin's supply line in the narrow pass.

Sima Qian describes what Han Xin did next. At night he sent two thousand light horsemen, each carrying a red Han banner, to hide in the hills near the Zhao camp. He then placed ten thousand men with their backs to a river, a position every manual condemned. The Zhao officers laughed when they saw it.

At dawn Han Xin advanced with his own flags and drums, fought, then fell back to the troops at the river. The Zhao army poured out of its camp to finish him off. But with the river behind them, Han Xin's soldiers had nowhere to run and fought desperately. Meanwhile his hidden cavalry rode into the empty Zhao camp, tore down the Zhao flags and raised two thousand red banners. Seeing them, the Zhao troops believed their camp and king were taken and broke. Chen Yu was killed and the king of Zhao captured.

Asked afterward, Han Xin cited the military classics: put soldiers on deadly ground and they will survive.
lesson: Keeping an easy way out can weaken commitment. Sometimes the best way to get full effort from yourself or a team is to remove the fallback.
source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), chapter 92
caveat: Sima Qian's figures for the size of the Zhao army are probably exaggerated.
